standard.title: Sample Space and Probability
standard.description: identify the sample space for single-stage events; assign probabilities to the outcomes of these events and predict relative frequencies for related events
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can assign probabilities on a 0–1 scale using fractions, percentages and decimals (from AC9M6P01). Students have experience with probability language and listing outcomes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify sample spaces for single-stage events, assign probabilities to outcomes, and use these to predict relative frequencies.

nodes.label: Identifying and listing sample spaces
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students identify the sample space for a single-stage event and list all possible outcomes systematically.
nodes.minimum_width: List the sample space for a coin toss and a standard die roll; explain what sample space means.
nodes.typical_width: List sample spaces for spinners, lucky dips, and card draws; verify the sample space is complete by confirming all outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
wider: Investigate sample spaces with unequal likelihood outcomes — can outcomes still be listed even if not equally likely?
Compare sample spaces for different versions of the same game (6-sided vs 8-sided die).

response_modes.reason: Systematic, complete listing of a sample space is prerequisite to assigning probabilities. Students who list incomplete sample spaces assign wrong probabilities to all outcomes.

nodes.hinge_reason: An incomplete sample space produces wrong probability fractions for all outcomes in Node 2 — if an outcome is missing from the sample space, every other outcome gets an inflated probability and the probabilities cannot sum to 1.
success_criteria: Lists a complete sample space for a given single-stage event.

nodes.label: Assigning probabilities to outcomes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students assign theoretical probabilities to outcomes of a single-stage event using P = favourable/total and express these as fractions, decimals or percentages.
nodes.minimum_width: Assign the probability of each outcome for a fair die roll; express as a fraction.
nodes.typical_width: Assign probabilities for events with unequal outcomes (e.g. spinners with unequal sectors); express in fraction, decimal and percentage forms; verify probabilities sum to 1.
wider: Investigate non-fair devices: if a spinner has sectors of 1/4, 1/4, and 1/2, assign probabilities and verify.
Connect probability fractions to relative frequency: a probability of 1/6 means in the long run about 1 in every 6 outcomes.

response_modes.reason: Students often believe probability only applies to fair devices. Encountering non-fair devices (biased coins, unequal spinners) generalises their understanding.

success_criteria: Correctly assigns the probability to each outcome in a sample space.
Verifies that all probabilities sum to 1.
Expresses probability in the most appropriate form for the context.

nodes.label: Predicting relative frequencies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use theoretical probability to predict how often an outcome will occur in a given number of trials.
nodes.minimum_width: Predict the number of times an outcome will occur in 60 trials given its probability.
nodes.typical_width: Predict relative frequencies for multiple outcomes; compare predictions to simulated results; explain discrepancies.
wider: Investigate how the accuracy of predictions improves with more trials — connect to AC9M7P02.
Apply relative frequency prediction to real decisions: fairness of a game, likelihood of an event occurring.

response_modes.reason: Predicting relative frequencies requires connecting probability, multiplication, and the meaning of the sample space — integrating all prior nodes.

success_criteria: Correctly predicts the relative frequency for a given number of trials.
Understands that predictions are expected values, not certainties.
Can adjust predictions for non-fair devices.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting theoretical probability to relative frequency prediction, and then to the law of large numbers, is a rich conceptual bridge — advancing students can reason about what probability actually means for real outcomes.
